title: Πίθηκος καὶ κάμηλος
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 306. Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἐν συνόδῳ τῶν ἀλόγων ζῴων πίθηκος ἀναστὰς ὠρχήσατο.
sentences.tr: En synodōi tōn alogōn zōiōn pithēkos anastas ōrchēsato.
sentences.l: In an assembly of the speechless animals a monkey, having stood up, danced.
sentences.n: τὰ ἄλογα ζῷα, 'the animals without λόγος' — without speech and without reason — is the ordinary Greek term for beasts, and it is quietly funny in a fable where they hold a meeting. The same opening begins fable 38, where a dancing monkey is elected king. ἀναστάς is the intransitive aorist participle of ἀνίστημι, 'having got to his feet'.

sentences.t: Σφόδρα δὲ αὐτοῦ εὐδοκιμοῦντος καὶ ὑπὸ πάντων ὑποσημαινομένου, κάμηλος φθονήσασα ἐβουλήθη τῶν αὐτῶν ἐφικέσθαι.
sentences.tr: Sphodra de autou eudokimountos kai hypo pantōn hyposēmainomenou, kamēlos phthonēsasa eboulēthē tōn autōn ephikesthai.
sentences.l: And he being exceedingly well thought of and being signalled to by all, a camel, having grown envious, wished to attain the same things.
sentences.i: He was very much admired, and all of them signalled their approval, so a camel out of envy wished to achieve as much herself.
sentences.n: ὑποσημαίνομαι is a rare verb, 'give a signal', and what gesture the animals made is not recoverable; the context makes it a sign of approval, so the literal line keeps the bare 'signalled' and the idiomatic line reads the context. φθονέω takes the dative of the person envied; ἐφικνέομαι takes the genitive of what is reached. κάμηλος is feminine here, as the participles show.

sentences.t: Διόπερ ἐξαναστᾶσα ἐπειρᾶτο καὶ αὐτὴ ὀρχεῖσθαι.
sentences.tr: Dioper exanastasa epeirato kai autē orcheisthai.
sentences.l: Wherefore, having sprung up, she too tried to dance.
sentences.n: The imperfect ἐπειρᾶτο is the tense of an attempt in progress, and here of one that does not succeed.

sentences.t: Πολλὰ δὲ αὐτῆς ἄτοπα ποιούσης, τὰ ζῷα ἀγανακτήσαντα ῥοπάλοις αὐτὴν παίοντα ἐξήλασαν.
sentences.tr: Polla de autēs atopa poiousēs, ta zōia aganaktēsanta rhopalois autēn paionta exēlasan.
sentences.l: And she doing many absurd things, the animals, having grown indignant, beating her with clubs, drove her out.
sentences.i: But she did many absurd things, and the animals in indignation beat her with clubs and drove her out.
sentences.n: ἄτοπος is literally 'out of place'; of behaviour it is unseemly, absurd. ἀγανακτήσαντα and παίοντα are neuter nominative plural, agreeing with τὰ ζῷα. The plural verb ἐξήλασαν is the regular exception to the rule that a neuter plural subject takes a singular verb: where the subject is a set of living creatures, Greek often counts them as individuals.

sentences.t: Πρὸς τοὺς διὰ φθόνον κρείττοσιν ἁμιλλωμένους ὁ λόγος εὔκαιρος.
sentences.tr: Pros tous dia phthonon kreittosin hamillōmenous ho logos eukairos.
sentences.l: Against those who out of envy contend with their betters the story is well-timed.
sentences.i: The story is well aimed at those who out of envy set themselves against their betters.
sentences.n: ἁμιλλάομαι takes the dative of whom one contends with; κρείττοσιν is the comparative of ἀγαθός used absolutely, 'the stronger, the better'. No verb is expressed in the moral — ἐστί is left to be understood, as it constantly is.
